Indigenous Americas refers to the native peoples and cultures of North, Central, and South America before, during, and after European colonization. This spans from the sophisticated civilizations of the Aztec and Inca to the countless smaller nations across the continent. In literature, the term encompasses both pre-Columbian oral traditions and written texts, and the later twentieth-century recovery and assertion of indigenous voices and histories in the face of centuries of colonial erasure and violence. Indigenous American themes—land, identity, cultural survival, and spiritual knowledge—have become central to Latin American and North American literature.

The Americas prior to 1492 were home to millions of people across hundreds of distinct cultures, linguistic groups, and political formations. It was not a wilderness but a complex, populated world. European colonization devastated indigenous populations through violence, enslavement, and above all epidemic disease such as smallpox and measles, which killed an estimated ninety percent of native peoples in many regions. Indigenous oral traditions and codices, pre-Columbian written records, preserved mythology, history, and knowledge systems fundamentally different from European frameworks.

Miguel Asturias and other twentieth-century Latin American writers recovered indigenous narratives and challenged the European colonial narrative of the Americas. Indigenous American worldviews—cyclical time, sacred landscapes, spiritual ecology—offered alternatives to Western rationalism and linear progress. These influenced modernist and postcolonial literature. Contemporary indigenous American literature explicitly reclaims voice and agency, centering indigenous perspectives in their own stories rather than as objects of European observation. The literary and historical study of indigenous Americas reveals colonialism not as a bringing of civilization but as a catastrophic interruption and theft.

Miguel Asturias is a Guatemalan author whose work centers indigenous Mesoamerican culture and colonial violence. Smallpox in the Americas is the pandemic that initiated the demographic catastrophe and is central to understanding indigenous historical trauma. Colonialism is the historical framework within which indigenous American literature operates as a counter-narrative. Caribbean literature is another region shaped by indigenous dispossession and the cultural synthesis of indigenous, African, and European traditions. Magical realism is a literary mode through which indigenous American and Latin American writers encode non-Western knowledge and temporality. Latin American literature is the literary tradition within which indigenous American voices have increasingly claimed space. The Aztec Empire was a major pre-Columbian civilization whose legacy indigenous literature retrieves and transforms.
